title: Figure and axes, and saving
summary: plt.bar() draws on “the current chart”. Real programs name it instead: fig, ax = plt.subplots() gives the figure (the whole picture) and the axes (the chart inside it). Draw with ax.bar(), label with ax.set_title(), size it with figsize, and save it with fig.savefig().
objectives: Make a figure and axes with plt.subplots().
Draw and label on ax: ax.bar(), ax.set_title(), ax.set_xlabel().
Save the chart as a PNG picture with savefig().

slides.h: By the end: a chart saved as a picture
slides.say: A chart for a report or a web page has to be a file. The figure is the picture you save; the axes is the chart drawn on it. Naming both is how every chart from here on is written.
points: `fig, ax = plt.subplots()`: figure first, then axes.
p: A chart for a report or a web page has to be a file. The figure is the picture you save; the axes is the chart drawn on it. Naming both is how every chart from here on is written.
`fig, ax = plt.subplots()`: figure first, then axes.

visual.text:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
df = pd.read_csv("weather.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(df["Month"], df["Rain_mm"])
ax.set_title("Rain, month by month")
ax.set_ylabel("Rain (mm)")
fig.savefig("rain.png")

slides.say: `plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))` makes the picture 8 wide and 4 high (in inches). Twelve months fit better on a wide chart; a sideways bar chart of ten wards on a tall one.
points: Wide for time; tall for long lists.

slides.say: `fig.savefig("name.png")` writes the picture into the folder, where a report or web page can use it. On your own computer, save **before** `plt.show()`: closing the window clears the chart, and a later save is blank.
points: Name files for what they show: rain.png, wards.png.
p: `fig.savefig("name.png")` writes the picture into the folder, where a report or web page can use it. On your own computer, save **before** `plt.show()`: closing the window clears the chart, and a later save is blank.
